content:
Only 2% of B2B buyers say their vendors look genuinely different.

Let that land. 

We asked 100 marketing leaders how often they think "these all basically do the same thing" while comparing vendors. 98% said at least sometimes. 61% said often or constantly.

Just 2% rarely or never feel it.

So sameness isn't an edge case. It's the default experience of buying B2B software. And it's really the sum of all the decisions companies have made over the years.

Nobody sets out to sound generic. It happens one approval at a time. The bold line gets flagged as "too aggressive." The competitor callout gets cut as "not on brand." The sharp claim gets hedged because legal wants it safer. Each edit is reasonable. The sum is a homepage that could belong to any of your competitors.

Differentiation isn't a copywriting task you delegate down. It's a risk you authorize from the top. The blandness in your messaging is the blandness you were willing to approve.

Your buyers can't tell you apart because you decided it was safer that way.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 4 days ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

content:
When B2B vendors look the same, buyers go looking for the difference. And they get frustrated when they can't find it.

We asked 100 marketing leaders what they do when the shortlist feels interchangeable. 

The #1 move, 41%, is to push for a trial or demo. They want to see the difference with their own eyes, because the website never spelled it out.

Here's one VP who told us why she picked one tool over two rivals: "their AI use cases were clearly stronger. Drift felt legacy with 'AI' bolted on, and Chili Piper's use cases were super broad."

That's the level of differentiation buyers want. Named, compared, concrete.

But almost no website talks like that. Most vendors hedge. They won't name the competitor. They won't take the sharp position. So they default to "AI-powered, automate your workflow, close more deals", and disappear into the sea of sameness.

Your buyers aren't asking you to be louder. They're asking you to be specific about who you beat and why.

Say the thing your competitor can't.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 week ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

content:
41% of B2B buyers say they chose a vendor for a genuinely different product capability.

Which raises a harder question: what about the other 59%?

We asked 100 marketing leaders the single biggest reason they picked the winner. 

Product capability led at 41%. But right behind it: easiest to buy from (24%), existing relationship or trust (21%), price (12%).

The easy story is that buyers are irrational. They say they want the best tool, then pick on feelings.

I don't buy that. These are senior operators.

Here's the likelier explanation: for most of them, a real product difference wasn't on the table. When you've already established the tools do basically the same thing, "which has the better capability" stops being a useful question. 

So you fall back to what's left, who's easier to work with, who you trust, who costs less.

That's not buyers being soft. That's buyers being rational in a market where vendors failed to build, or failed to prove, a real difference.

The 59% is a differentiation problem. Or maybe brand opportunity.

87% of B2B buyers get to a vendor through a peer recommendation.

72% already knew the vendor before the search started.

"Their messaging stood out"? 29%. Fourth place.

We used Wynter to ask 100 marketing leaders what actually gets a vendor onto their shortlist.

The thing that gets you considered is other people talking about you, and having been around long enough to be familiar.

So the questions worth asking: how many of your customers are happy enough to put their name on a recommendation? How easy do you make it for them to do it? And are you consistent enough, long enough, to be the vendor people already know when the search begins?

You get shortlisted by being the one people already trust.

content:
64% of buyers said it is hard to tell competing vendors apart.

We used a Wynter survey to ask 100 B2B marketers about vendor comparison.

What the research shows is that most websites fail to communicate meaningful differentiation. Majority constantly thought "these all basically do the same thing".

When everything reads the same, buyers split. 56% dug deep to find a real difference. The other 44% gave up trying and decided on other factors.

One CMO stopped using vendor material entirely: "I stopped reading and using their info and looked to my peers for insights and recommendations on the tool(s) they use. That was far more informative than anything I got from any of the vendors."

So when the website doesn't make the difference clear, what closes the deal?

Two things, neck and neck.

1. 32% said it came down to fit. 

Whoever proved they matched the exact use case, stack, and integrations won.

2. 31% said the sales experience was the real difference. 

A rep who explained what the site couldn't. As one CMO put it: "their sellers were able to do a good job of explaining the differences that the website by itself was not able to do."

Companies are scared (or stupid?) to not focus on their differentiation. If they're lucky enough to still get a demo request, it's then up to the salespeople to explain it. But all but the best-known brands get just ignored.

content:
68% of Google searches now end without a click... to *anywhere.*

That finding comes from my co-author Rand Fishkin’s latest research, and yes, it’s a doozy. But before you spiral into "is SEO dead?" — don't.

Because the click was never the point. It was just the thing we could measure.

For years, we treated traffic like the scoreboard. More sessions meant the strategy was working. Less traffic meant something was broken.

But if Google, AI Overviews, Amazon, social feeds, and AI tools are increasingly filtering, ranking, summarizing, and recommending before a person ever lands on your site, then the job changes.

You don’t just need to "get the click."

You need to become the brand people and machines look for by name.

I wrote up what I’d actually do about it:

• who's still winning Google's clicks, and why it's not just "better content"
• why AI-referred visitors may be fewer but more valuable
• why branded search, owned assets, and correlation dashboards matter more than traffic charts
• the 3 bets I'd make that survive every algorithm update

I regret to inform you that clicks probably aren't coming back. But you can build marketing that still works when they don’t.

content:
"How would you start a marketing strategy from scratch?"

(Real question I got in a webinar this morning, and I didn't have a chance to answer it, so I'm answering it here.)

The annoying but true answer is: it depends. Obviously. But because that's less fun, I would start with one question:

1) How is this business supposed to grow?

Is the intended growth mechanism raw discovery?

Meaning: people have a problem, they search for it, and we need to show up.

Cool. Then SEO, comparison pages, and educational content probably matter a lot.

Is it product-led growth?

Meaning: users become a force multiplier, and they ultimately need to share the product with others or use the product more frequently in order to gain more value?

Then onboarding content, use-case content, templates, lifecycle emails, and activation loops probably matter more.

Is it sales-led?

Meaning: the business depends on reps reaching out, building relationships, educating prospects, and moving accounts through a long buying process.

Then the first content priority might be the sales asset the team has been begging for, like a buyer guide or follow-up email sequence.

2) After this, I would look for the shortest path to proving marketing can help. It might look like:

• Discovery-led motion → fix the highest-intent pages
• Sales-led motion → create the asset sales needs this month
• Product-led motion → improve the content that shortens time-to-value

Of course, the long-term work matters. You still need the bigger strategy — the category POV, event program, content engine, etc. 

But early on, marketing needs to earn internal trust. The fastest way to do that is to understand how the company grows, then make that motion work better.

content:
"What's our AI visibility like?"

If my CEO or CMO asked me that, here's what I'd do.

First, run our brand through HubSpot's AEO Grader. Then summarize what stands out.

I did this for SparkToro.

The report correctly identified us as a niche audience research tool. And it picked up on one of our biggest advantages: credibility with marketing practitioners.

That's affirming because it confirms what I already suspected.

Other parts need a human read:

The competitive set is messy. SparkToro gets compared to Semrush, Ahrefs, Similarweb, Brandwatch, and more. Some are fair nearby alternatives. They're not all direct competitors. But this info is useful — because it shows how AI is categorizing the brand, even when it gets that wrong. And if AI believes something off about you, well… odds are part of your audience does too.

The share of voice info requires nuance. SparkToro shows up at 24% in ChatGPT and Perplexity, but just 12.5% in Gemini — where Semrush and Similarweb both rank higher. Our prospects might currently believe we all have the same offerings even though we don’t.

The growth areas were plausible but generic: more enterprise features, more integrations, more automation. Useful? Sure. But you could advise that for most SaaS companies.

So here's what I’d do next:

1/ Find what's accurate.
What is AI already getting right? For us: audience research, credibility among marketers, ease of use and affordability, unique insights, and credible data sources.

2/ Find the misconceptions.
Where is AI putting us in the wrong category, comparing us to the wrong tools, or understating what we do?

3/ Turn the gaps into priorities.
That's a to-do list for website copy, content, PR, sales enablement, and category education.

Then run this analysis again in 1-2 months to see what moved.

HubSpot AEO Grader is a free way to see how your brand shows up across AI tools — what's resonating, and what you still need to clarify.

Jay Acunzo has talked for a long time about "resonance over reach."

And I agree with him. Don't just chase impressions. Don't optimize every idea for the biggest possible audience. Don't water down your work until it's broadly legible but mostly forgettable.

Reach without resonance is just noise.

But... for marketers, we don't get to opt out of reach.

I think what we really need is sequencing — resonance BEFORE reach. 

Make the thing specific enough to matter, spread, and be remembered. Our work still has to travel, but it travels further when it actually means something to someone first. 

Jay and I talk about this on this week's episode of Zero Click Marketing, plus:

• why public speaking is the original zero-click channel
• why marketers need to become better arguers for their ideas
• how to make work that people actually remember.

content:
A new AE on my team closed 16 deals in her second month. The team average is 8.

Here’s how she did it:

1. She focuses on the customer’s main priority on call 1. "What would you say is the most important challenge or goal that you’re looking to solve with a solution like Deel?" It’s a simple question. But it sets the table for the entire sales process and how she differentiates herself from competitors.

2. She ties every demo click back to those priorities and challenges. "You mentioned [specific pain] earlier. Here's exactly how that gets handled." Every feature becomes about them and what they’re looking to accomplish, not the product.

3. For pricing concessions always come with a give/get. "I can do that if we extend the contract term to two years. Is that something that works for you?" That way she doesn’t lose any power and her negotiations are always a partnership.

4. She’s not afraid to hard close. "If I can get you to [price], can we sign by [date]?" No hypothetical negotiations. Either she has a deal or she has a real objection.

5. She summary closes every late stage call. "So we have [pain], we solve it with [outcome], the investment is [price]. Is there any reason we shouldn't move forward?" Either gets the commit or surfaces the real objection. No follow up limbo.

6. She lets the buyer build the demo. "Before I show you anything, walk me through what would make this demo a success for you." Now she only shows what matters. Demos get shorter and tighter.

7. Arms the champion to sell internally. She stopped hoping the champion could sell for her. She used to send a deck and trust they'd present it right. Now she builds an Aligned room with the ROI, the recap, and a one page business case ready to forward. The CFO sees the deal the way she'd present it.


And that my friends.

Is how you close 16 deals in your second month.

content:
The problem with a lot of AI is that it's supposed to make us more efficient, but we spend huge amounts of time trying to get it to produce what we're looking for, when we could've just created it manually faster to begin with.

Especially with images.

Thumbnails are something I've been creating manually since I started my first YouTube channel in 2011.

But it's also a piece of my content workflow that, if it worked well, I'd be totally guilt-free handing over to AI. 

But I’ve never been able to find anything that solved three things at once:

1. Maintaining a true likeness of the person in the video
2. Keeping brand guidelines incorporated
3. Actually saving time/repeatably generating good results, instead of just swapping editing for prompting and re-prompting time.


A few weeks ago I tried Luma AI and it nailed the first two.

Photorealism: I could take a screenshot of a podcast guest from a Zoom recording and turn it into an image that looked ready for a YouTube thumbnail.

Brand: Paste in a screenshot of brand guidelines and an example from a previous podcast thumbnail, and it would replicate them near perfectly.

But I was still swapping Photoshop or Canva for an AI editor. 

Now, it works as a board vs a traditional chat, so it’s easy to click/reference/pull from multiple images to teach it what I wanted, which works great, but I wasn’t really solving for the third problem (becoming more efficient). 

Then last week, Luma released the API for their Uni-1 model, which I started playing with over the weekend and it’s finally solving the time-saving problem, which has always been my biggest complaint with AI image generation. 

Now I can build thumbnail generation straight into a Claude skill, using the exact parameters I was already using to make them manually.

And because that Claude skill is already pulling timestamps from the transcript for other content, thumbnails get generated automatically the moment a new podcast gets recorded. 

To test it out, I set it up to see if it could repeatably create Colin and Samir-type thumbnails (in our branding with our guests) with nothing but a podcast transcript and screenshot. 

Turned out pretty spot on.

content:
Meredith asked a great question (it’s around the 1:40 mark in this clip). What are some ways sellers can work WITH procurement instead of against procurement. 

Certainly, bringing in early is clutch. It allows us to deliver value well beyond price.

As a procurement guy, my job is not to secure the lowest price. First and foremost my job is to find (source) the best tool relative to the needs of company and then structure an optimized contract accordingly. Buying the right tool. Selecting the right SKU. Purchasing the right number of licenses. Structuring the right SLAs. This is how we balance enabling our stakeholders while being the fiduciary looking after our spend (and often why we report to finance). . It’s way it’s so much more than price (strong SLAs, payment terms, clauses and terms that help with enablement and performance). 

This is why on-going discovery is so important. You need to find out what’s important to us and then digging deep to get to the right answer (the interest behind the position)f. Of course, buyers and sellers will often start out guarded. But those walls can come down and a beautiful partnership can form.  

I've seen it happen.  It's hard to get there.  But worth it.  

P.S.  In preparing for this, the podcast team put all the prep and information in a deal room.  As a procurement guy, I'm a huge fan of this... and yet I don't see it near as often as I'd like.

The top 10 invisible consequences of working at a toxic company:

1. Shortens your life.

Workplace psychological issues shorten lifespan by up to 3 years. 

2. Destroys your sleep. 

76% of employees report work-related stress negatively impacts their sleep. 

3. Weakens your immune system. 

Chronic workplace stress suppresses immune function. People in toxic jobs get sick more often and recover slower. 

4. Erodes your self trust. 

Toxic work environments train you to second-guess yourself, people please, and stop trusting your own judgement. 

5. Follows you home. 

People experiencing high levels of stress at work carry that home, leading to strained relationships with family and friends. 

6. Drives unhealthy coping. 

Toxic work environments increase risks of turning to unhealthy coping behaviors like smoking, drinking, and overusing medication. 

7. Kills creativity. 

Fear of judgement from unsafe work environments is a top factor that reduces creativity and innovation. 

8. Lowers productivity. 

43% employees in toxic work environments spend more time trying to look productive than actually producing meaningful outputs.

9. Causes anxiety and/or depression. 

87% of people who experienced a toxic work environment said it negatively impacted their mental health. 

10. Damages your heart. 

Workplace stress increases the risk of cardiovascular disease by 1.6X and risk of heart attacks by 2X. 

__

content:
Imagine trying to tell Gary the factory worker that he should learn to use a computer and make money with his brain. It's 1975. His plant just started implementing industrial automation.

He's been working there for 22 years. Good wage. 20 more years and he retires with a pension.

He can see the headcount shrinking. Some of his friends at other plants already got laid off.

So he's working harder than ever. Coming in early. Staying late. Learning every new machine they bring in.

But skilled physical labor was being automated. The premium moved up a level to the people who could think, analyze, strategize, and manage. Knowledge work commanded a value that physical labor no longer could.

Four years later, Gary was laid off and struggled to find his footing in the new economy.

__

Now consider that many people reading this are Gary.

They've spent 5-20 years building a career as a knowledge worker. Making good money. Respected in their field.

Their company started implementing AI in 2023.

They can see their team shrinking. Friends at other companies are getting laid off.

So they're working harder than ever. Starting early. Available late. Learning every new AI tool they can find.

But knowledge work is being automated. The premium is moving up a level again to the people who have developed what AI cannot replicate. Clarity. Self-trust. Emotional Sovereignty. Judgment. Creativity. Deep Human Connection. Presence. Adaptability.

The shift isn't about working harder or learning more tools to do knowledge work better.

It's about elevating to the next level. Again. 

The premium skills of the future are built in your nervous system, not in your mind.

__

And I get it. Saying this to a knowledge worker right now probably sounds just as foreign as someone telling Gary to learn how to use a computer and make money with his brain in 1975.

What a Series A fundraising announcement would sound like if people told the truth:

"I am proud to announce that we have sold 20% of our company to XYZ Venture Labs for $30M at a $150M valuation."

It seems like we're rich now, but I didn't make any actual money. I'm still eating Ramen and grinding 996. Now my salary is capped at whatever the board approves. My title is Founder but I make a lower salary than the average mid-level manager. 

We are going to scale hard. Like real hard. And by scale hard, I mean we will increase spending 10X and waste a majority of the money on things that don't drive any customer value. 

We will run out of money again in 18 months. I'll spend half my time building decks for investors instead of leading my company or driving value for customers. 

We raised at a $150M valuation. Sounds impressive, right? That is 100X our ARR. Even though a majority of our revenue isn't real ARR. 

The median public and private market comps are about 4X. So we are overvalued by something like 25X. 

We'll need to grow revenue from $2M to $100M just to clear our current liquidation preferences. 

There is a 30% chance I get fired as CEO by my own board. 

There is a 75% chance we spend 5 to 10 years building this company and literally make zero dollars. 

And there's a 90% chance our investors consider our company a failure because it doesn't generate returns that actually matter to the fund.

But I am dedicated. And this is going to be huge. 

That's what I'm telling myself. And that's what I'm telling LinkedIn. 

And now this post is going to get 1,000 likes with everyone congratulating me for what is statistically a really bad decision. 

Our startup is going to the moon 🚀  

p.s. we just opened 80 new roles for our brand new office. Yes, our lease costs almost as much as our annual revenue, but duh culture. Like we are a family. We get tattoos of our company. And work 7 days per week. Who has time to sleep when you have to slave away to drive real returns for your VC overlords??? I've helped position over 500 companies, and have boiled it down to three core strategies that anyone can learn in ten minutes. 

The concept is simple: 
People love putting tools in buckets. 

You can put your tool in a bucket that everyone knows...
You can put your tool in an bucket that only a small group of people know...
Or you can say my tool is in a brand new bucket that I invented.

The downstream impacts of these three strategies are HUGE. 

They essentially determine how you'll go-to-market, what you compete with, and where your differentiation lives.

content:
Spoiler alert: Everything in marketing works.

I've done over 300 hours of interviews with CMOs and VPs in B2B marketing. I spent a decade as a marketing leader myself (before officially become a thought leader) and I can tell you this one thing:

Everything in marketing works.

YouTube works. LinkedIn works. Direct mail works. Webinars work. TikTok works. Email works. Events work. PR works. Partnerships work. Heck, even spending $75k with Gartner can work.

But the challenge is figuring out which channels can work for you with the ingredients you have.

You don't always have the product, the features, the timing, the wind at your back, the talent on the team, the budget. But that is the fun part about the job in marketing - you get be the chef, but sometimes there's only two eggs, a slice of bread and an onion left in the fridge. Can you work with that?

The other thing that matters is the strategy. Why are you doing this. What are the goals, what is your POV on it, and how can you pull it off?

Too often we try to do everything - all those channels above - because we think we have to. And the result is another B2B YouTube channel with 30 videos that all have between 17 and 62 views. You'd be better off picking one channel and doing DEEP there and then finding ways to stack those wins into other channels.

This type of thinking has always been a guardrail on the teams I've been on:

- What's in it for me?
- Why should someone open this email?
- Why would someone actually take an hour out of their day and attend your webinar? Would *you* actually go to this webinar?
- Would you respond to that message?
- Would you see that ad and click on it?

And last thing - this is the hardest one. Often times GOOD MARKETING is not good for the company. That's right. It's harder to measure, takes time, not obvious, doesn't have UTM parameters in link; there might not be a direct response call to action. And that's what makes it good and makes it work, but you need to have the patience to trust it - and the ability to stand up in front of the CEO/CFO and articulate the marketing strategy and why you do things the way you do.

What did miss?

PS. If you are reading this and work in marketing, your job is to embrace this. Treat your job like a craft. Have conviction. Don't follow best practices. Use your brain.  Be creative. Disrupt things inside of your company and push for a new way of doing things. More important now than ever when everyone has access to the Slop Machine ™️

We write about this stuff weekly at: exitfive.com/newsletter
